notes.b: Many sports need a player to change direction suddenly without losing control. That skill is agility, one of the six components of performance-related fitness (the fitness qualities that help a person perform well in a sport).
points: Definition: agility is the ability to change the position or direction of the body quickly and with control, while keeping balance.
Rugby: a ball carrier side-steps (steps sharply to one side) to evade a tackler. This is agility because the direction changes quickly and the player stays in control.
Badminton: a player recovers to the centre of the court after each shot and changes direction to reach the next shuttle (the feathered shot that is hit over the net).
notes.tip: Agility includes a change of direction with control. Running fast in a straight line is speed, not agility. If asked to define agility and outline its importance in a named activity, give the definition and then a specific moment in that activity.

notes.b: Balance is what stops you toppling over, whether you are still or moving. It comes in two types, and exam answers should name both.
points: Definition: balance is the ability to keep the body's centre of mass (the point around which its weight is evenly spread) over its base of support (the part of the body in contact with the ground).
Static balance: balance while stationary, such as holding a handstand or an arabesque (a ballet or gymnastics pose standing on one leg with the other leg lifted behind).
Dynamic balance: balance while moving, such as a gymnast travelling along the beam or a hurler striking the ball on the run.

notes.b: Most skills need several parts of the body, or the eyes and the body, to work as one. Co-ordination is how well they do that.
points: Definition: co-ordination is the ability to use two or more body parts, or the senses and body parts, together smoothly and efficiently.
Hurling: hand-eye co-ordination (the eyes guiding the hands) is needed to strike a moving sliotar (the hurling ball).
Front crawl: the swimmer must time the arm pull, the leg kick and the breathing so that they work together.

notes.b: Power combines two other qualities: how strong a movement is and how fast it is done. A strong but slow movement is not powerful.
points: Definition: power is the ability to apply strength (the force a muscle can produce) at speed; power = strength × speed.
High jump: the explosive (very fast and forceful) drive of the take-off leg, which pushes the jumper upwards.
Shot-put: the rapid extension (straightening) of the legs, trunk and arm at release, when the shot leaves the hand.
Badminton: the smash, a hard, fast downward shot.
notes.tip: Strength is health-related in the specification, while power is performance-related. Write power as strength × speed, not as strength alone.

notes.b: Speed is about how quickly the whole body, or just one part of it, covers a distance. It can be measured, which is why it has a formula.
points: Definition: speed is the ability to move the body, or a part of it, from one point to another in the shortest possible time; speed = distance ÷ time.
Whole-body speed: a 100 m sprint, or a basketball fast break (a quick attack up the court before the defence is set).
Limb speed (the speed of an arm or leg alone): the speed of the arm in a throw or of the leg in a kick.

notes.b: Reaction time measures how quickly you start to respond, not how quickly you finish. To avoid mixing it up with the movement itself, learn it alongside movement time and response time.
points: Definition: reaction time is the time between the presentation of a stimulus (the signal that prompts a response) and the start of the response.
Movement time: the time from starting a movement to completing it.
Response time = reaction time + movement time, so response time covers the whole action from signal to finish.
Sprinting: reacting to the starting gun.
Soccer goalkeeping: reacting to a shot or a deflection (a ball that changes direction after hitting a player or post).
Two examples in one activity, tennis: reacting to the opponent's serve, and reacting to a volley (a shot hit before the ball bounces) at the net.
notes.tip: Reaction time ends when movement starts. It does not include the movement itself. If asked for two examples of where it is needed, give both from one named activity.

notes.h: Identifying the main component for an event
notes.b: Exam tables describe an athlete or event and ask which component matters most. Work out what the athlete actually has to do, then match it to a component.
points: A 100 m breaststroke swimmer needs speed and power off the start and turns, where a fast, forceful push is needed.
A tennis server needs power and co-ordination, because the serve combines a forceful strike with well-timed movement of the body and arm.
A goalkeeper needs reaction time, agility and power, to respond to a shot, change position and dive or jump.
Justify the choice by linking the component to a specific moment in the event.
notes.tip: You may be asked to identify the main component for named athletes or events, explain each choice, and name another activity where it matters. You may also be asked for two components important in one named activity, with a justification for each.

questions.prompt: Identify two performance-related components of fitness important in a named physical activity and justify their importance.
questions.model: Activity: soccer goalkeeping. 1. Reaction time: the time between the stimulus and the start of the response. A goalkeeper has a fraction of a second to respond to a close-range shot or a deflection, so a short reaction time decides whether they get a hand to the ball. 2. Power: strength applied at speed. The goalkeeper must spring explosively sideways or upwards from a set position to reach shots in the corners and to claim high crosses above attackers.

questions.prompt: Define reaction time and give two examples of where it is needed in one physical activity.
questions.model: Reaction time is the time between the presentation of a stimulus and the start of the response. In badminton it is needed to respond to a smash aimed at the body and to react when the shuttle clips the net and changes direction.
